At 1:48PM, my friends and I were walking along the popular jogging trail to do some naturalizing and came across this pair nesting close together in the grassy area dotted with small trees and flowers adjoining the trail. It was around 76 degrees F, and getting warmer as the time passed. There were no other visible ducks in the vicinity at the time, but plenty of insects flying about. The larger one seemed to be the male with its heavier face details, and the smaller one that stayed close to it is the female of the pair. They both stood up as we approached, and the male was wary of us, and tried to keep the female behind him. However, once they realized that we had Hawaiian rolls with us, they were much more relaxed and took turns eating. The male even pooped in our presence.

At 2:30PM, I was sweating up a storm in the humidity (77 degrees F) as my cousin and I started to walk along the jogging path that goes behind the houses that line West Oaks Boulevard. This area is mostly lined with grass and trees that overhang over the fences that line one side of the path, and the drainage creek that lines the other side. The Muscovy Duck population (they number around 20-25 individuals) in this neighborhood often flock to this area to rest because they're less likely to be disturbed by the human inhabitants. This particular drake came up very close to me (less that a foot away) as I was trying to take a picture of the rest of the flock that was busy fighting for food 20ft away. Why was this one trying to come to me when I obviously had no food? I got a very nice picture of it in the end though.

description: Today (08/27/2018), at 7:24 pm I observed a Muscovy Duck in Tampa, Florida on the University of South Florida campus. The Muscovy Duck (a deuterostome), originally named the "Musco Duck" is a wild, non-native species to Florida. Its scientific name is Cairina moschata. During my observation, it was moderately hot (79F), cloudy, humid and slightly windy. The duck was walking near a large lake surrounded by tall trees and a grassy area. This particular duck interacted with organisms of the same species. It walked adjacent to a small group of other Muscovy Ducks, straying away on occasion but always returning to them. The duck was quiet and seemed to be very calm. It had just exited the water so it was drying its feathers. Through my observation, I noticed that the duck had a black and white speckled neck and dark body. It had patches of green feathers on its body as well. Its most distinguishing characteristic was the red bumpy flesh surrounding its eyes and beak. I read two articles that helped me identify this duck. One was published by the Fort Myers Florida Weekly and the other was published by Countryside Daily. Both articles mentioned the uniqueness of the red bumpy flesh surrounding the organisms face.

description:
The Muscovy duck is scientifically known as the Cairinia moschata and it belongs to the family Anatidae. Living in Florida, we have all seen these ducks roaming around near ponds or on the sidewalks at one point or another. These ducks are originally from South America, and are not considered true ducks because “all true ducks originate from the Mallard, but the Muscovy does not” (raising-ducks.com). Their habitat consists of coastal and lowland areas where lakes, lagoons, marshes, or slow moving streams are present. Although it is easy to identify a Muscovy duck due to their red warty faces, today there are so many different colored ones that have a small distinct feature that it me lead to a small doubt when one is spotted. When these ducks reach adulthood, it becomes easier to spot a male versus a female because males are larger than the females (raising-ducks). A fun fact about these ducks is that they are the quietest of all poultry. The temperature at the time that I took this picture was 89 degrees.

I saw this while just walking around the Crescent Lake and ducks covered every square meter, and they had absolutely no fear of humans  (except for 1 or 2 mallards). This one was solitary, and stood near the small lake (that’s the thing which appears to be completely white back there, I turned up the brightness to much, sorry.) in the grass. Their are 3 quite distinct things about this duck that make it differ from other ducks that waddled around hoping for bread crumbs. The most obvious one is the fleshy, growth stretching from the eye to eye and over the beak. My guess is that it’s for display because I can’t discern any other purpose for it. Tied with that is the pattern of there body with coloring being being black with patches of white around the tail and and wings and the neck being the opposite color scheme but with black spots on the back of the neck and black spots scattered around the plumage on the back of the birds neck and head. Now because another species of duck had similar looking plumage (still easily discernable from each other.). Of course he looks like an average duck or goose body, long neck and a ovalish body with tail feathers. Id say the duck came up to right below my knee in height. Anyways, this duck seemed slightly more confrontational (in the way he a way to “intimidate” someone ulike than other ducks) species around it or at because it has three distinct behaviors which happened once I got near, with 2 happening at once(not on purpose mind you).
1. It started to make some kinda sound and it’s plumage rose.
2.it started to wag its tail feathers like a dog would wag its tail which was quite strange to see. 
My guess is that these are his sign for “hey back away, I don’t like you”. Other than that though he just kinda stood there. As you can see he’s standing in some grass next to an average tree which happens to be right by a very much fitting place for a duck to be, a lake.

description:
Muscovy Duck: Deuterostome
"Truly wild individuals are restricted to south Texas and points south, but domesticated versions occur in parks and farms across much of North America. Wild Muscovy Ducks are glossy black with bold white wing patches and are forest dwellers that nest in tree cavities. Their range expanded into Texas in the 1980s; feral populations also exist in Florida." (all about birds)
They are large ducks. Females are considerably smaller though, and only grow to 6.6 pounds; roughly half the males' size. The bird is predominantly black and white, with the back feathers being iridescent and glossy in males, while the females are more drab. The amount of white on the neck and head is variable, as well as the bill, which can be yellow, pink, black, or any mixture of these.

description:
The Domestic Muscovy Duck has green, black, and white feathers. It has red around its eye and had brown baby chicks. This observation was made at 3:40pm on Oct. 25, 2019. The habitat that this Ducks was found is on USF Tampa campus. The Habitat around where I found the Ducks is known to have natural woodlands and wetlands environment which is home for many animals, insects, and plants. (https://www.hillsboroughcounty.org/library/hillsborough/media-center/documents/emergency-management/09--pdrp-environmental.pdf)
Identified for confirmation through the website : https://animaldiversity.org/

Visually, the Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) had a variation of color on its feathers, ranging from bright white patches (especially on its underbelly) to dark green and black iridescent feathers along its sides and wings covering its back. This distribution of coloration may serve as an ecological advantage to blend in with the water from predators/ dangers from above while being able to blend in with the surface of the water/ light streaming in from predators swimming below. Additionally, I observed that the duck two had short legs with webbed orange feet and red patches on its beak area. While I was unable to see any reproductive structures from my viewpoint, male Muscovy ducks tend to display greater iridescent green feather coloration as an inter-sexual selection for a demonstration of greater fitness during breeding times. The disparities between male and female reproductive structures for this species lies in the differentiation in gametophytes, as in most reptilia, the male duck will have the sperm and through mating will transfer their genetic information to the female to be fused with her ova and produce a fertilized zygote. Characteristics present in this observation as defining traits for the Muscovy duck to be part of the taxonomic Clade Deuterostomia, Phylum Chordata, Subphylum Vertebrata, and Class Reptilia are the presence of a backbone (vertebrae), the fact that this species employs the use of amniotic eggs for reproduction, and the lack of gills/ presence of feathers that demonstrate adaptation to terrestrial environments. Additionally, while these traits couldn’t be physically seen, as a deuterostome defining embryonic characteristics of the duck that make it part of this taxon include radial cleavage in the oocyte and the development of the mouth at the opposite end from the blastopore in the embryo (the blastopore becomes the anus). A reference website with a description of the organism is Neotropical Birds website (https://neotropical.birds.cornell.edu/Species-Account/nb/species/musduc/overview) that provides information regarding the appearance, behavior, and breeding of this species. The habitat in which I made my observation was around a pond that had plenty of exposure to sunlight and various types of vegetation growing around it such as reeds and aquatic plants that I observed in shallower regions of the pond. I made this observation in the temperate climate of Tampa, Florida and nearby patches of trees seemed to be locations where the ducks went to rest in the shade. The Muscovy duck is native to Mexico, Central, and South America but small feral populations have migrated north and east to settle and develop populations in Florida.

description:
Cairina moschata, also known as a Muscovy duck, is a deuterostome that can grow anywhere from 2.1 to 2.5 feet in size and is typically characterized by its warty red face. Muscovy ducks can be black, white, blue, chocolate, bronze, and lavender, but they often contain multiple colors. They also can have orange or black webbed feet to help them swim in ponds, lakes, or other bodies of water. This duck is commonly found in South America but is also seen in parts of southern North America as well. They often live and breed in wooded habitats along lakes, marshes, mangrove swamps, and slow-moving streams. Their diet typically consists of grasses, water lily seeds, mangrove seeds, insect larvae, spiders, worms, mollusks, small fish, and more. They use their bill to dig into the surrounding ground to grab any food that may lie there. An interesting detail about the Muscovy duck is that they build their nests in cavities and hallows of mature trees. A female may stay with only one nest site for her entire lifetime. These ducks are typically found in pairs, but individuals still often have multiple mates. The males perform a courtship dance to impress the female to mate with them, and the males are also known to get aggressive with one another.

description:
Visual Description: 
This bird has dark brownish green color feathers and has white spots around its body. It has a red coloring around its eye. Its beak is a dark brown color with white spots and a tan colored tip. 
Horizontally, the bird is about 1-1.5 ft long and vertically, it is about 1 ft tall. Its beak is about 1-1.5 inches long. The birds legs are short and its feet are webbed. Its tail is short. 
The birds were in a group- about 10 of them. They were not making any noises. The bird was walking around and picking at the ground with its beak looking for food or eating. Also, the bird would move its tail back and forth quickly every couple minutes. 

Habitat: The birds were found in an urban area- on USF's campus in an open area with some trees spaced out. They were walking about in a mostly dirt area with some grass. The birds were about 20-30 ft away from a lake.

The bird may be a Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata), an introduced species to urban and suburban areas of Florida. However, they are typically found in lowlands from northern Mexico south, west of the Andes, to southwestern Ecuador and, east of the Andes, to northeastern Argentina and Brazil.

References: https://myfwc.com/wildlifehabitats/nonnatives/birds/waterfowl/muscovy-duck/

The organism depicted above is a Cairina duck. The genus of this particular species of duck is Cairina, which is part of the chordate phylum. This organism is considered a deuterostome, due to its classification of chordate. Phenotypically, the duck is mostly black with some distinctive white spots and a white neck. The climate that these ducks tend to be located in tropical climates, hence its origin in South America. These ducks, however, can adapt to cooler climates during migration times. The size of the duck is relatively intermediate compared to other organisms, with the male weighing up to 15lbs. Being that of a chordate, they produce sexually with female ducks, producing viable and fertile offspring. The life-span for such a species is estimated from about 7-8 years. The behavior of such ducks is usually timid unless when the mother is being protective of her offspring.

These ducks tend to live in various lakes and ponds and can be seen thriving in the water of Castor Beach. Muscovy Ducks are native to Mexico and South America, but have been predominantly found in Florida.

description:
Visual Description: This Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) was heavy-bodied and about a foot and a half long. This animal walked low to the ground and had flat webbed feet that were an orangish color. This duck had a long neck and tail, and its body had many different colors including shades of green, blue, brown, and white. This Muscovy duck had a white head with brown spots and its black eyes were surrounded by a bumpy red region. In addition, this animal had a slim white/ light pink bill that was about an inch long and it had some brown dots on it. 

Defining Characteristics: This organism is a deuterostome. Deuterostomes are different than protostomes because their anus develops before their mouth or any other opening in the embryonic stage. Muscovy ducks are known for being large and full-bodied and they have long necks that resemble geese. They have a long bill and multi-colored feathers. Their tails are long and throughout their body there are various shades of blue, green, brown, white, etc. Muscovy ducks have red rigid coloring around their eyes and have webbed feet that are flat.

Habitat: This duck was seen on the sidewalk on the USF campus near a pond. The habitats of these ducks include streams, ponds, lakes, rivers, and more. Muscovy ducks are normally found near water that is slow moving and are commonly seen in urban areas including golf courses, retention ponds, parks, and more.

Habitat: Commonly found in this area, a corner patch of grass along the western sidewalk south of the parking garage. Usually in the field south of the garage, or sleeping in groups near the sign at the southmost entrance to the garage.

Description of Observation: While walking on the sidewalk on the USF Tampa campus, this duck was located walking back and forth in the area pacing, before sitting down and remaining seated for the remainder of the encounter.

Defining Characteristics: Black feathers and bright red facial "mask."

Time of Length of Observation: 5 minutes.

description: I had never been to Meditation Park before which is a small park along a canal in between a hospital, busy roadways and residential areas. Unfortunately the area is poorly maintained with trash everywhere. There was signs of homeless encampments in a few places and lots of moldy clothes strewn all over the place. description:
A solo visit, rather last-minute. There was a report the night before about 2230 on the main Florida birding Facebook group about a possible Tufted Duck at Lake Morton in Lakeland. I decided to chase it. This morning, by 0730, before I left, two European birders had commented that the duck was a hybrid, with Tufted Duck being one parent and either a Ring-necked Duck or a Lesser Scaup being the other parent. Clearly, this news massively dampened enthusiasm for chasing the duck. I'm sure that 60+ birders who had packed their cars last night had decided to stay home once the duck was identified as a hybrid. Birders can be funny about that oftentimes ... I decided to chase the duck regardless, since it was reasonably close (less than a 90-minute drive), I had nothing else planned today, and it's always fun to see all the swans, geese, and other exotic waterfowl -- and the native species too. I arrived at 1030 and the ONLY other birder present was John Cima, who had discovered the duck about a week ago. If not for the two posts this morning, probably 100 birders would have descended on the park today. The weather at the start was sunny and 67 degrees ("feels like" 67) with a light breeze. When I left at 1230, it was sunny and low 70s with a light breeze.

I parked at the southeastern corner of the lake and walked  counter-clockwise, since the light was better than walking clockwise. I _tried_ to tally every individual of every bird species present, but it is nearly impossible given the amount of birds and the fact that I was concentrating (as always) of photographing as many birds as I could.

My camera, a Panasonic Lumix FZ80 (my sixth, I think) quit working yesterday; the camera turns off when I try to zoom in (it has 60x, zoom, which I use to the maximum). It's still under warranty, so I need to send it back. To my surprise, returning home yesterday, I found an old Lumix FZ80 (maybe my fifth) that I had forgotten about, sitting on a shelf in my closet. The exposure knob no longer functions -- a known defect with this camera model, in my experience -- but a faulty camera with a functioning 60x, zoom is 1,000,000 times better than no camera or a camera with no functioning zoom.

The first few dozen images I took today, in bright sunlight in my standard "Intelligent Auto" setting, were quite dark (the exposure "broke" in a very dark setting). I deleted most of these images, since I do not believe in editing images (other than cropping) that I upload to iNat. I experimented with other settings. To my surprise and delight, the "SCN" setting -- for scene selection -- proved to be a wonderful alternative, taking images that were beautiful in shade and only slightly (at times) overexposed in direct sunlight. Overall, I was quite pleased with this camera today -- I took more than 1,200 photographs here and at Colt Creek State Park, where I visited after leaving Lakeland!

If I have posted multiple records of a species, then I am positive or nearly certain that they represent multiple individuals. Selected bird species and estinmated numbers at Lake Morton Park follow:

White Ibis: 300+, with 95% in adult plumage

Mallard: I quit counting quickly, but I estimate 75-100 in a typically massive degree of variation in plumages. I did not see any Mallards that I thought were back-crosses with Mottled Ducks, but I marked two males as "Mallards, Pintails, and Allies."

Mute Swan: 35-40, with two active nests with eggs

Black Swan: 20-25, with 2 nests with eggs and a pair with two cygnets. NOTE: why can't I "count" the eggs or cygets as wild birds from "captive" parents? According to iNaturalist guidelines referencing captive plants or animals, the progengy of these individuals should be "countable" and Research-Gradable. Right? Or wrong?

American White Pelican: 60, mostly in one flock. At one point, a dozen or more individuals fed in a flock literally along the shoreline, less than 15 feet from where I was standing, taking videos. American White Pelicans are noisy when foraging!

Swan Goose: 1, seemingly not a hybrid/back-cross.

Graylag Goose: 1, seemingly not a hybrid/back-cross.

I did not see either of the two Black-necked Swans or the single Coscoroba Swan that were present in previous years; apparently they are now dead.

I took a ton of photographs of the putative Tufted Duck hybrid. Additional comments on Facebook since I took my photographs suggest that the duck may simply be a very worn female Lesser Scaup. Accordingly, I am listing it as "Scaups, Pochards, and Allies."

description: The main focus of this observation is the organism that appears to be a duck. I identified this organism scientifically to be the Cairina moschata domestica.

The duck has a robust, medium to large body, with a black-and-white plumage. Its feathers are primarily dark, with iridescent greenish-black hues, and there are patches of white, particularly visible on its wings. The bird also has a unique facial structure, characterized by red, bumpy, fleshy growths known as "caruncles" around the base of its bill and on its face. Its bill is pale, and its legs are a dull, orange-brown color.
A defining characteristic of the Muscovy Duck is its caruncles, which are common in adult males and some females, making them easily identifiable. The species is also known for its relatively quiet nature compared to other ducks, often producing soft hisses instead of quacks. I came across this Muscovy Duck when I went On a walk on the Tampa USF campus, the duck was walking around the grasses and crossing the concrete side-walk. The Muscovy Duck (Cairina moschata) is native to Central and South America, particularly in forested and swampy areas. Its natural range extends from Mexico down through Argentina. In the United States, Muscovy Ducks are often found in the wild in southern states like Florida and Texas, where feral populations have become established, particularly in urban and suburban environments.

description:
For my Muscovy Duck observation, I captured a group of wild Muscovy Ducks near a water body. These ducks are a distinctive species, known for their predominantly dark plumage with iridescent highlights and white facial patches. They are native to Central and South America but have established wild populations in various regions.

The observation included clear photographic evidence and an initial identification as Cairina moschata. Upon submission to iNaturalists, it was classified as a casual grade observation. After review and confirmation by the community, it reached research grade, validating the accuracy of the identification. The ducks were observed in their natural habitat, adhering to the project’s requirement to document only wild organisms.
